use /lib
from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/new-project import NewProjectScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope
from /ui/components/right-sidebar import RightSidebarScope

export scope ModeSystemPromptsScope:
    concept: {ModeSystemPromptsConcept}

concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of
        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        What a prompt tells the harness besides itself comes in two parts. The
        system template is the conversation's system prompt: the same for
        every prompt of a conversation, whatever its mode, so the harness's
        prompt cache holds when the mode changes. Each lane's tasks, and the
        questions, carry on a conversation of their own, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, and each fills the system template in
        for what its runs can see, so it stays the same within each. Each of the
        @{PromptModesScope} but Freeform has instructions of its own, which
        change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own
        message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. A
        prompt's hidden anchor has a systemPrompt property, alongside its
        userPrompt, holding its mode's instructions.

    templates:
        The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected
        prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they
        can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a
        dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

        - CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says
        - HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
        - SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
        - PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
        - UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

        SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are
        filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but
        UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the
        task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is
        given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file,
        and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or
        removed, like any other text of a template.

        A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can
        see, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. A run of the spec
        lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code
        location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and
        system template alike. A question can see the code location and the
        spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code
        lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task,
        runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.

        A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with
        nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or
        SPEC_LOCATION filled in with nothing goes too, whatever else it says,
        so no prompt names, or tells the harness to keep off, a location its
        run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled
        in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence
        pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template
        left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at
        all.

        HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt,
        as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, reads its agentic Markdown and
        reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for
        Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the
        directories the @{NewProjectScope} names for them.

    readingTheSpec:
        In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its
        compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under
        HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions,
        and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what
        `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use.
        It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what
        the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system
        template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec
        location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec
        location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is
        told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or
        from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A
        question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec
        location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice`
        reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question
        says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the
        spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled
        reference, with nothing about the spec source.

    writingTheSpec:
        Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec,
        work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file
        only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can
        edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check
        the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the
        source again.

    pitonFluency:
        The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in
        the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of
        the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.

        It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the
        project's data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, each time the
        application runs a spec build in the project, as the @{SpecBuildScope}
        says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its
        FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has
        ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What
        it prints is written as text, never read as Piton.

        PITON_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Spec instructions
        and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a
        paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation
        before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec
        is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is.
        The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a
        Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.

        Where `piton` isn't installed, or printing the fluency fails, no file
        is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the
        paragraph pointing at it is left out.

    specReading:
        The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing
        anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled
        reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they
        name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected
        into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may
        itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as
        written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING
        filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own,
        saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, in
        spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet the project uses its default.

    codeToSpec:
        The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says, after the Spec instructions. It may use
        every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and
        two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as
        it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or
        with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is
        taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each
        project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the
        templates, and edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet
        the project uses its default.

        The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a
        Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with
        SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its
        spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

    saving:
        Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected
        prompts, saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, a
        Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md,
        combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited
        in the @{SettingsWindowScope}. One with no file yet gives its default.

    understandingFile:
        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
        the @{RightSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each
        constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never
        to the spec's source.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a
        project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are
        baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships
        with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults
        the next build has. A build can't be made without them.

        The system template's default says what the project is, where its
        code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the
        one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a
        <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it
        may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds
        no fluency.

        The spec-reading prompt's default says:

        \\
